Central Nervous System
Histology
Neuron, Nerve fibers, Nerve trunk

This lesson covers the histological building blocks of nervous tissue: the neuron and its two functional processes (axon and dendrite), how neurons are classified by shape, process number, and axon length, and the microscopic organization of a nerve fiber and nerve trunk. Central themes include the ultrastructure of the neuron cell body (Nissl bodies, organelles, cytoskeleton), the structure and staining of the myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier, and how connective tissue layers (endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium) bundle nerve fibers into a peripheral nerve trunk.

Histological Classification of Nervous Tissue

Nervous tissue is classified according to structure into two components:

  • Nerve cells (neurons) — conduct electrical impulses.
  • Glial cells (neuroglia) — support and protect neurons.

The Neuron

The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It consists of two main parts: the cell body (soma/perikaryon) and its processes, which may be axons (conduct impulses away from the cell) or dendrites (receive stimuli toward the cell).

Cell Body (Soma/Perikaryon) — Light Microscopy

  • Size: variable, 5–150 μm in diameter.
  • Nucleus: single, large, spherical, centrally located; pale-staining (vesicular) with a well-defined nucleolus.
  • Nissl bodies (granules): abundant basophilic granules in the cytoplasm, well stained by basic stains (e.g. toluidine blue). They are free ribosomes and ribosomes attached to RER, and synthesize the neuron's proteins. They are absent from the axon hillock and axon, around the nucleus, and at the cell periphery. Their degeneration is called chromatolysis.
  • Golgi complex: located around the nucleus (the perikaryon); demonstrable with silver stain.

Cell Body — Electron Microscopy

Nucleus: abundant euchromatin.

Organelles: a well-developed perinuclear Golgi complex; numerous mitochondria scattered through the cytoplasm; well-developed RER and free ribosomes (seen as Nissl bodies at LM); and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER), abundant and extending into axons/dendrites in most neurons — its function is unclear but may relate to synaptic vesicle transport.

Cytoskeleton: neurofilaments (intermediate filaments, ~10 nm, abundant throughout the neuron), microfilaments (actin, ~6 nm, associated with the cell membrane), and microtubules (~24 nm, scattered in the soma cytoplasm). Functions: maintain cell shape, transport neurotransmitter vesicles from the Golgi complex to nerve endings, and transmit nerve impulses.

Inclusions: melanin granules (in some CNS neurons, e.g. substantia nigra of the midbrain — function unknown), lipofuscin granules (increase with age; accumulated lysosomal activity product), glycogen granules, and lipid droplets.

Centrioles are absent, since mature nerve cells do not divide.

Axon vs. Dendrites

FeatureAxonDendrites
NumberSingleMultiple
LengthLongShort
ThicknessThin, constant diameterThick with wide base, tapering end
ContourRegularIrregular
BranchingTerminal arborization; few collaterals at right anglesExtensive branches at acute angles; some bear dendritic spines (gemmules) acting as synaptic sites
CytoplasmMitochondria and neurofibrils only — no Nissl granules, no Golgi complexAll structures of the cell body except the Golgi complex
ConductionCentrifugal (away from cell body)Centripetal (toward cell body)

Classification of Neurons

I. Morphological Classification

By number of processes:

  • Unipolar — single process; rare in vertebrates (mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve).
  • Pseudounipolar — rounded cells with a single process that convolutes (forming a glomerulus) then divides in an inverted T-shape into a dendrite and an axon; site: dorsal root ganglia.
  • Bipolar — spindle-shaped, two processes from opposite poles; sites: cochlear ganglia, retina, olfactory epithelium.
  • Multipolar — one axon and many dendrites; the most common type.

By shape of the nerve cell:

  • Pyramidal — in the cerebral cortex.
  • Pyriform — large, flask-shaped, e.g. Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.
  • Polygonal / stellate — e.g. anterior horn cells of the spinal cord.

By size and axon length:

  • Golgi type I — large cells with long axons, e.g. pyramidal cells of the cerebral cortex.
  • Golgi type II — small cells with short axons, e.g. interneurons of the spinal cord.

II. Physiological Classification

  • Sensory neurons — receive stimuli from the internal/external environment and conduct to the CNS.
  • Motor neurons — conduct impulses from the CNS to muscles and glands.
  • Interneurons — connect sensory and motor neurons with each other.

Nerve Fiber

Nerve fibers are the axons of nerve cells. Histologically, a nerve fiber consists of three parts: the axon, the myelin sheath, and the neurolemmal sheath.

Axon (Axis Cylinder)

Has a constant diameter along its length with few right-angle collaterals; its cytoplasm (axoplasm) is surrounded by the axolemma. It is divided into three segments:

  • Axon hillock — the first short pyramid-shaped segment; lacks Nissl bodies but contains many microtubules and neurofilaments.
  • Initial segment — between the axon hillock and the start of myelination; contains microtubules and neurofilaments.
  • Axon proper — the rest of the axon; lacks Nissl bodies and Golgi complex but contains mitochondria, SER, microtubules, and neurofilaments. Terminates in terminal arborization, each branch ending in a terminal end bulb/button rich in mitochondria and neurosecretory vesicles.

Myelin Sheath

A whitish lipoprotein covering of the axon. It is not continuous — it is interrupted by gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The distance between two successive nodes is the internodal segment (0.2–2 mm). Each internodal segment shows several oblique clefts in the myelin called clefts of Schmidt-Lanterman, where cells between the myelin lamellae provide conduction of nutrition to the deeper layers of myelin and to the axon.

Staining of myelin: H&E dissolves the myelin sheath, which appears as an unstained space around the pink axon. Myelin stains black with osmium tetroxide (surrounding an unstained axon).

Cells responsible for myelination: Schwann cells in the PNS; oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

Functions of the myelin sheath: insulation; acceleration of nerve conduction; protection and nutrition of the axon.

Neurolemmal Sheath

Consists of a chain of flattened Schwann cells forming a tube around the axon. The cells have flattened nuclei and a small amount of cytoplasm containing a small Golgi complex and few mitochondria. Schwann cells are covered externally by a basal lamina and a thin delicate connective tissue layer called the endoneurium. The sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier.

Classification of Nerve Fibers by Myelination

TypeMyelin sheathNeurolemmal sheathExample
Naked fibersAbsentAbsentGray matter of the CNS
Unmyelinated with neurolemmaAbsentPresentSympathetic fibers
Myelinated without neurolemmaPresentAbsentNerve fibers of white matter of the CNS
Myelinated with neurolemmaPresentPresentPeripheral nerves

Nerve Trunk

A peripheral nerve (nerve trunk) consists of bundles of nerve fibers together with a connective tissue component, organized into three concentric layers:

LayerLevel of organization
EpineuriumDense connective tissue surrounding the whole nerve trunk; formed of collagen and elastic fibers with fibroblasts.
PerineuriumSurrounds each bundle (fascicle) into which the nerve trunk is divided.
EndoneuriumDelicate connective tissue layer surrounding each individual nerve fiber; in contact with the basal lamina of the Schwann cell.

Staining of the nerve trunk (histological appearance):

With H&E: the axon appears as an acidophilic structure surrounded by an empty space (dissolved myelin), itself surrounded by a thin pink rim of Schwann cell cytoplasm.

With osmic acid: the myelin sheath stains black while the axon remains unstained, appearing as an empty space.

With silver stain: the axons appear specifically brown.

Key Points / Quick Review

Nervous Tissue & Neuron

  • Nervous tissue = neurons (conduct impulses) + neuroglia (support/protect).
  • Neuron = cell body + axon (efferent) + dendrites (afferent).
  • Nissl bodies = RER/ribosomes; absent in axon hillock, axon, perinuclear zone, and periphery.
  • Chromatolysis = degeneration of Nissl bodies.
  • Centrioles absent — mature neurons don't divide.

Axon vs. Dendrite

  • Axon: single, long, constant diameter, no Nissl/Golgi, centrifugal conduction.
  • Dendrite: multiple, short, tapering, has all soma organelles except Golgi, centripetal conduction.

Neuron Classification

  • By processes: unipolar, pseudounipolar (DRG), bipolar (retina, cochlear, olfactory), multipolar (commonest).
  • By shape: pyramidal, pyriform (Purkinje), polygonal/stellate (anterior horn cells).
  • By axon length: Golgi I (long axon, cortex) vs Golgi II (short axon, interneurons).
  • Physiological: sensory, motor, interneurons.

Nerve Fiber Structure

  • Axon parts: hillock → initial segment → axon proper → terminal arborization.
  • Nodes of Ranvier interrupt the myelin sheath; internodal segment 0.2–2 mm.
  • Clefts of Schmidt-Lanterman = nutritional channels within myelin.
  • Schwann cells myelinate PNS; oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS.
  • Myelin functions: insulation, faster conduction, protection/nutrition.

Myelination Staining

  • H&E: myelin dissolves (unstained space); axon pink/acidophilic.
  • Osmium tetroxide: myelin black; axon unstained.
  • Silver stain: axons appear brown.
  • 4 fiber types by myelin/neurolemma combination (naked, unmyelinated+neurolemma, myelinated−neurolemma, myelinated+neurolemma).

Nerve Trunk Layers

  • Endoneurium — around each individual nerve fiber.
  • Perineurium — around each fascicle (bundle of fibers).
  • Epineurium — around the whole nerve trunk.
